Pakistan committed to implementing Saudi.headline: Pakistan committed to implementing Saudi defence pact, Makkah agreement: FO
Pakistan committed to implementing Saudi.summary: Pakistan on Thursday said it remained committed “in intent and spirit” to implementing the Strategic Mutual Defence Agreement (SMDA) with Saudi Arabia and the trilateral Makkah Defence Alliance. Foreign Office (FO) spokesperson Sajjad Haider Khan made the statement during his weekly briefing. The statement comes amid renewed tensions in the Middle East, with Yemen’s Houthi rebels carrying out attacks in Saudi Arabia in recent days. A day earlier, a Saudi-led coalition battling Houthis accused the rebels of targeting the holy city of Makkah, sparking outrage across the Muslim world and deepening the conflict roiling the region. However, the Houthis swiftly rejected Riyadh’s report as a “lie” that it shot down a drone from the rebels heading towards Makkah. In response to a question on whether “any mechanism had been devised as to how Pakistan will ensure that recent Houthi attacks in Saudi Arabia are thwarted,” the spokesperson said that Pakistan was committed to “implementing” the SDMA and the Makkah pact. “However, when, how, where and what force will be used against what objectives, in which modes and matters [..] — operational confidentiality requires us to be discreet at this stage,” he added. Asked about the diplomatic efforts undertaken by Pakistan to “de-escalate and defuse” the Houthi issue, the spokesperson said, “Pakistan has for a long time [..] shared the perspective that we would like to have peace and stability because this is not only in the interest of Pakistan and Iran, but also the entire region and beyond.” Khan termed the situation in Bab al-Mandeb “exceptionally serious” and went on to call on the Houthis to “stop their activities”. “In this regard, our discussions basically revolve around bringing peace and stability through dialogue and diplomacy and not through coercive measures,” he added. PM Shehbaz to head to US next week for UNGA In his press briefing, the spokesperson also confirmed that Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif will be leading Pakistan’s delegation at the 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly (UNGA) in New York next week. Khan said that the premier will be accompanied by Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar and several federal ministers. FO said that in his address at UNGA, PM Shehbaz will “highlight Pakistan’s perspective on regional and global developments, reaffirming the importance of dialogue, diplomacy and restraint and peaceful resolution of issues”. He said the premier is also expected to outline Pakistan’s priorities on sustainable development, climate change, counter-terrorism, Islamophobia, global economic challenges, UN reforms and issues concerning the Global South. He will also draw attention to the situation in India-occupied Kashmir and Palestine, the FO spokesperson said. He added that on the sidelines, PM Shehbaz is scheduled to participate in high-level events and hold bilateral engagements with world leaders and the UN secretary general, where he will highlight “Pakistan’s commitment to multilateralism, the UN Charter, regional peace and international cooperation”. ‘Malicious media campaign’ against Pakistan on Sikh pilgrims The spokesperson was also asked about media reports regarding Pakistani Sikh pilgrims who were stopped at Faisalabad International Airport while travelling to India to perform religious rituals at Gurdwara Sri Hemkund Sahib. In response, he termed it a “malicious media campaign” on India’s part and clarified, “It was reported that the pilgrims were not allowed to board the plane, which is not correct.” “We were not aware that the Indian High Commission had issued these visas, and the visas were not covered under the 1974 bilateral protocol that exists between Pakistan and India,” he said, explaining that protocol’s objective was to facilitate visits to shrines between both countries. Khan said the visas were issued “independently of any coordination”. Noting India’s “exceptionally restrictive visa regime,” the spokesperson said Pakistan was committed to “extending a warm welcome to Sikh pilgrims in Pakistan, including from India”. He also cited the number of visas issued to Sikh pilgrims over various religious occasions, stating that the “numbers speak for themselves”. He noted that Indian Sikh pilgrims had been barred by their country from travelling to Pakistan in 2025. Khan also maintained that Pakistan was ready to welcome Sikh pilgrims through the Kartarpur corridor “as and when India allows them because it has been closed from the Indian side and not Pakistan”. Khan was also asked about India’s participation at the 12th meeting of the Heads of Border Services of the Competent Authorities of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO). In this regard, the spokesperson confirmed that India’s chargé d’affaires was present at the summit. “Participation is there, and we hope that participation will continue because the broader objective is peace and security and fighting terrorism, and it is a common challenge for both countries.” On being asked about India’s response to Pakistan and China operationalising a joint mechanism for managing their common border, the FO spokesperson rejected India’s “baseless and illegally untenable assertions” on the development and the Joint Boundary Demarcation Commission. The Joint Boundary Demarcation Commission was established under the Sino-Pakistan Boundary Agreement of March 2, 1963. According to India’s NDTV, the country’s external affairs ministry had called into question the legality of the commission. “China is not only our neighbour but an all-weather strategic corporate partner. Our ironclad ties have withstood the test of time,” he said. He stressed that the 1963 agreement was “valid”. Khan said that it was a “mockery of international law that India spoke of legality in an attempt to challenge the validity of the border commission”. At this, he said the country should first “carry out its own introspection” over actions in India-occupied Kashmir “instead of advancing fictitious territorial claims”.

India to take 'all necessary measures' t.headline: India to take 'all necessary measures' to protect economic interests after US passes Russia sanctions bill
India to take 'all necessary measures' t.summary: India said on Thursday it would continue buying oil from “diversified” suppliers, after US lawmakers approved sanctions designed to squeeze Russia over its war in Ukraine. The US legislation targets Russia’s energy and defence sectors, President Vladimir Putin and other senior officials, as well as Moscow’s so-called shadow fleet of tankers used to circumvent Western sanctions. It also gives US President Donald Trump authority to impose tariffs of up to 100 per cent on major buyers of Russian oil and gas — including potentially China and India — in an effort to choke off revenue financing Moscow’s war. But India’s foreign ministry said it “remains firmly committed to ensuring energy security for its 1.4 billion people”. “It will continue to do so through diversified sourcing and on the basis of evolving market dynamics.” Moscow is one of New Delhi’s most important strategic partners and military suppliers. “The Indian side has also made clear its determination to take all necessary measures to protect its trade and economic interests,” the ministry added. India has navigated the energy crisis caused by the US-Iran conflict in part by turning to Russia, despite Moscow’s war in Ukraine and pressure from Washington and other Western capitals. Putin and Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi held talks in New Delhi last week ahead of a Brics summit. “This issue has been discussed at high levels in recent months with various US interlocutors,” the ministry added. “Its potential implications for not just the bilateral relationship but also the international energy market have been very clearly articulated by the Indian side.” Indian refiners nearly doubled crude imports from Russia to 2.25 million barrels a day in March — the weeks after the Middle East war erupted — helped by temporary US waivers. Shipments hit a record 2.81m in July, according to trade intelligence firm Kpler, but have since dropped back to 2.07m last month.

‘Belligerent action’: Pakistan protests.headline: ‘Belligerent action’: Pakistan protests Indian Navy vessel’s 'provocative' manoeuvre near PN vessel
‘Belligerent action’: Pakistan protests.summary: Pakistan on Wednesday summoned the Charge d’Affaires of the Indian High Commission and lodged a “strong protest” over a “highly provocative and unacceptable” action by an Indian Navy vessel in Pakistan’s Exclusive Economic Zone (EEZ) on Sept 15, the Foreign Office (FO) said. According to the FO, the incident occurred while the Pakistan Navy was conducting its biennial exercise, SEASPARK-26. The FO said that the Indian vessel carried out “aggressive manoeuvres” in dangerously close proximity to a Pakistani naval ship, resulting in contact between the two vessels. The ministry termed the incident a “serious violation of international law” as well as the 1991 bilateral agreement on Advance Notice on Military Exercises, Manoeuvres and Troop Movements. It said the incident also risked escalating tensions in the region. The Indian diplomat was asked to convey to New Delhi that Pakistan “strongly rejects” the “belligerent Indian action” and urged India to strictly adhere to international law and bilateral agreements, particularly those intended to prevent incidents at sea. The FO added that Pakistan’s Charge d’Affaires in New Delhi would lodge a similar demarche with India’s Ministry of External Affairs. Pakistan also called on the international community to urge India to refrain from what it described as “irresponsible actions” that could further destabilise South Asia. “The region can ill-afford to remain perpetually hostage to India’s reckless pursuit of conflict and instability,” the ministry said. India’s Ministry of External Affairs also summoned Pakistan’s envoy in New Delhi earlier today and issued a demarche over the incident. In May 2025, a four-day conflict between Pakistan and India was sparked by an attack on tourists in occupied Kashmir’s Pahalgam, which New Delhi, without evidence, linked to Pakistan. Islamabad strongly denied responsibility while calling for a neutral investigation. After New Delhi launched deadly air strikes in Punjab and Azad Kashmir on May 7, Pakistan said it downed six Indian planes in air-to-air combat, later raising the tally to eight. After tit-for-tat strikes on each other’s airbases, it took American intervention on May 10 for both sides to finally reach a ceasefire. In April, on the first anniversary of the Pahalgam attack, Pakistan had rejected a renewed Indian propaganda campaign linking it to the attack, deploring that the neighbouring country was focusing on “weaponising its false narrative” in the midst of a regional crisis sparked by the US-Israel war on Iran.

US drone maker Powerus says it signed Mo.headline: US drone maker Powerus says it signed MoU with Pakistan Army, gets initial order
US drone maker Powerus says it signed Mo.summary: US drone firm Powerus has signed a memorandum of understanding (MoU) with the Pakistan Army that includes an initial drone-related order, co-founder Brett Velicovich told Reuters on Wednesday. Velicovich declined to provide details, citing security sensitivities, but said the deal fell within the category of unmanned aerial systems. He also declined to disclose the value of the order, citing confidentiality. Powerus, which offers aerial and maritime drones for military and industrial use, is due to merge with a publicly traded company backed by two of US President Donald Trump’s sons, called Aureus Greenway Holdings. Both companies have said they expect the merger to complete in early October. Trump’s sons, Donald Trump Jr and Eric Trump, own a stake in Aureus through an investment fund called American Ventures, according to US regulatory filings. American Ventures is expected to hold a 9.9 per cent beneficial ownership stake in the combined company after the merger, regulatory filings show. Inter-Services Public Relations on Wednesday said a Powerus delegation led by Velicovich met Chief of Defence Forces (CDF) and Chief of Army Staff Field Marshal Asim Munir and they discussed defence procurement, production and long-term capacity building. The statement did not mention the MoU. The military’s media wing did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the agreement outside business hours. Andrew Fox, Powerus’ founder and chief executive, said that Pakistan’s private defence sector remains “emerging but still not mature”, leaving room for US firms to move faster. “The goal would be a joint technology relationship, pairing best-in-breed technology from the US with best-in-breed technology from Pakistan,” Velicovich said, adding that Powerus was exploring ways to potentially build technology in Pakistan. Fox dismissed suggestions that the company’s growth was linked to the involvement of the Trump sons, saying contracts were awarded on merit and that they had “no involvement on the business side” of the company. Donald Trump Jr was a passive investor with an indirect holding, his spokesperson said. “Don has no involvement whatsoever in the management or operations of Powerus and plays absolutely no role in the procurement of contracts in the United States or abroad,” the spokesperson said. “He had no prior knowledge of this deal and had no involvement of any kind in its negotiation, procurement or execution.” Eric Trump could not immediately be reached. White House Special Assistant to the President and Principal Deputy Press Secretary Anna Kelly said, “There are no conflicts of interest.”

Will respond to terror threats from Afgh.headline: Will respond to terror threats from Afghanistan in self-defence as and when needed, Pakistan tells UNSC
Will respond to terror threats from Afgh.summary: WASHINGTON: Pakistan told the UN Security Council on Wednesday that it would respond to terrorist threats emanating from Afghanistan in self-defence as and when needed and in accordance with international law. The assertion by Pakistan’s Permanent Representative to the United Nations Asim Iftikhar Ahmad came during a Security Council meeting on the situation in Afghanistan five years after the Taliban’s takeover of Kabul. “Pakistan cannot sit idle in the face of this terrorist onslaught,” Ahmad told the UNSC. “We will respond in self-defence, as and when needed and in accordance with international law. We will defend ourselves against whosoever attempts to harm our citizens and our national security.” He said that more than 4,700 Pakistanis had lost their lives to terrorism emanating from Afghanistan over the past three years and added that Kabul had failed to take concrete and verifiable action against terrorist groups operating from Afghan soil. Afghanistan had again become a safe haven for terrorist groups including the banned Tehreek-i-Taliban Pakistan, Baloch Liberation Army and its Majeed Brigade, Islamic State-Khorasan and the East Turkestan Islamic Movement, as well as their affiliates, Pakistan’s envoy said. “The situation [is] made worse by external actors, the spoilers who support proxies inside Afghanistan to target Pakistan and other neighbouring countries,” he added. A recent report by UN Secretary General Antonio Guterres says terrorist groups remain present in Afghanistan, while restrictions on women and girls, exclusionary governance, economic pressures, declining capacity to provide basic services and large-scale returns and migration continue to threaten the country’s longer-term stability. Armed groups opposed to the Taliban also remain active. According to the report, such groups claimed responsibility for 88 attacks across 21 Afghan provinces between May 1 and the end of July. The report identifies the institutionalised denial of the rights of women and girls and the authoritarian nature of the Afghan Taliban’s political system among the most serious concerns. It says these policies affect Afghan society and remain obstacles to the country’s reintegration into the international system. Against this backdrop, Ahmad said Islamabad had supported Afghanistan’s stabilisation through engagement, humanitarian assistance and regional cooperation. “Despite reservations with regard to certain policies of the Afghan Taliban, Pakistan abided by its international commitments to allow unhindered humanitarian aid to Afghanistan. As noted in the secretary general’s report, at least 687 humanitarian cargo trucks entered Afghanistan from Pakistan during the reporting period,” he said. But, “unfortunately, the hopes and expectations of the international community at that critical juncture five years ago did not materialise and in fact gradually turned into despair and disappointment”. “The extent of challenges in Afghanistan is evident … and the secretary general’s report highlights that the semblance of relative stability that the Taliban seek to display ‘masks the accumulating risks that could impact the country’s stability over the short and long term’“, he said. Ahmad said terrorism had been at the “core of Afghanistan’s problems”. “This finds its roots in the deep nexus between the Taliban and terrorist groups,” he said, adding that the Afghan Taliban had failed to act against the terrorist groups. He further warned about weapons left behind in Afghanistan by international forces and illegal arms trafficking. The United States took a similarly critical position on the Afghan Taliban, with Ambassador Mike Waltz focusing on the detention of American citizens, terrorism and restrictions on women and girls. “The United States will not tolerate the Taliban taking American citizens hostage. Period,” Waltz said, accusing the Afghan Taliban of using American citizens as bargaining chips. He called on the Security Council to condemn the detention of US citizens by the Afghan Taliban and demand their release. Waltz also criticised the Taliban’s sheltering of terrorist groups and cited UN reporting on arbitrary arrests and detention, torture, ill-treatment and extrajudicial killings. He highlighted the continuing ban on girls’ education beyond sixth grade and restrictions preventing Afghan women working for the United Nations from entering UN compounds. The envoy questioned how long the international community could continue relying on engagement without seeing concrete changes. “How many UN reports documenting abuse? How many Council resolutions demanding change? How many years of ‘engagement’ can we pass before we see measurable results?” he asked. “This Council must demand results from the Taliban,” Waltz said. “We need to see action, not words.” Russia, on the other hand, argued that engagement rather than pressure remained essential in Afghanistan’s case. Ambassador Vassily Nebenzia said there was “no alternative” to genuine, pragmatic engagement with Afghanistan. Recalling the withdrawal of foreign forces five years ago, he said predictions that Afghanistan would collapse or become a “black hole” had not materialised. Nebenzia attributed the country’s relative stability to the Taliban’s focus on development, regional cooperation and building a self-reliant state. He called for trust-based dialogue with the Afghan authorities, “fully free from the language of pressure and blackmail”. China also argued for continued engagement while acknowledging concerns over the treatment of women. Deputy Ambassador Sun Lei urged all parties to “cherish the outcomes of engagement and dialogue with the Afghan government, show good faith and stay patient”. But he said restrictions imposed on Afghan women and girls affected their physical and mental health and undermined social stability and development prospects, making it harder for Afghanistan to gain greater international support. China called on the Afghan rulers to guarantee the fundamental rights and interests of all Afghans, including women. Seemingly referring to the US, it called on a “relevant country” to “bear its historical responsibilities” by resuming aid to Afghanistan, lifting unilateral sanctions, returning the overseas assets of the Central Bank of Afghanistan and providing resources for the country’s reconstruction and development. The debate highlighted the central disagreement over how the international community should deal with Afghanistan five years after the Taliban takeover.

Security forces kill 3 terrorists in Bal.headline: Security forces kill 3 terrorists in Balochistan's Awaran district: state media
Security forces kill 3 terrorists in Bal.summary: Security forces killed three terrorists in an intelligence-based operation (IBO) in the Badrang area of Balochistan’s Awaran district, state-run Radio Pakistan reported on Thursday. A large quantity of weapons and ammunition was recovered from the possession of the terrorists of Fitna al Hindustan, according to security sources cited by Radio Pakistan. Fitna al Hindustan is a term designated by the state for terrorist organisations in Balo­chistan. Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi praised security forces for the “successful operation conducted under Operation Radd-ul-Fitna 3”, state-run APP reported. In a statement, the minister said the operation reflected the capability and commitment of the forces in dealing with security threats. He affirmed that security forces remain determined to maintain peace in Balochistan and continue efforts to counter terrorism. He noted that personnel deployed in different areas of the province were carrying out their responsibilities with commitment and resolve. Naqvi noted that security forces had once again foiled terrorists’ plans through timely action. The minister further said that the complete elimination of terrorists and their facilitators was the demand of the entire nation. He said all institutions were working toward this objective, and efforts will continue to address security challenges. Terror attacks in Balochistan Balochistan has witnessed an increase in terrorist attacks in recent weeks, prompting security forces to intensify counter-terrorism operations. Last month, the number of terrorist attacks in the province increased by seven per cent from 83 in July to 89 in August, according to a monthly assessment by the Pakistan Institute for Conflict and Security Studies. On the night of Aug 31-Sept 1, terrorists of the banned Tehreek-i-Taliban Pakistan (TTP) launched a coordinated attack on the Customs House, located at Ziarat Cross on the N-50 National Highway, in the Pishin district. In retaliatory action, security forces killed 10 terrorists while two officers were among six martyred in the fire exchange, according to the military’s media affairs wing. Also on August 31, 11 terrorists belonging to Fitna-al-Hindustan, who had blocked the N-40 Quetta-Taftan highway by establishing an illegal checkpoint for extortion in Chagai’s Nokcha area, were killed following an intense exchange of fire. On September 2, security forces killed 12 terrorists in the Kalat district during an IBO. Days later, the troops killed 11 terrorists and recovered 2.9 tonnes of explosives during separate IBOs in Kharan and Washuk districts. Another 36 terrorists were eliminated during multiple “high-tempo” operations conducted in Mastung, Quetta, Kalat and Sibi districts, the Inter-Services Public Relations said on September 4. These also included thwarting an attack on a police station in Sibi’s Bhag area. On Monday, nine terrorists, including a key commander of a banned outfit, were killed by security forces and the Balochistan Counter-Terrorism Department in two separate operations in Mastung, Pishin and Qila Abdullah districts.

Pakistan to stand by Saudi Arabia 'pract.headline: Pakistan to stand by Saudi Arabia 'practically and diplomatically' if Yemen conflict escalates: Asif
Pakistan to stand by Saudi Arabia 'pract.summary: Defence Minister Khawaja Asif on Wednesday said Pakistan would “practically and diplomatically” stand by Saudi Arabia against Yemen’s Houthi rebels if the situation escalated. Earlier in the day, the Saudi-led coalition battling Yemen’s Houthis accused the rebels of targeting the holy city of Makkah, sparking outrage across the Muslim world and deepening the conflict roiling the region. However, the Houthis swiftly rejected Riyadh’s report as a “lie” that it shot down a drone from the rebels heading towards Makkah. “If the situation escalates, we will stand with Saudi Arabia, both practically and diplomatically,” he said while speaking on Geo News programme ‘Aaj Shehzaib Khanzada Ke Saath’. Commenting on the Pakistan-Turkiye-Saudi Arabia trilateral agreement — the Makkah Defence Alliance — he affirmed that an agreement was in place. However, he said that even if there had been no such agreement, Pakistan was bound by an “eternal agreement to respond if the holy sites come under attack”. “There are some worldly agreements, too, and they have their own sanctity and obligations, but protecting the holy sites is our religious duty,” he said. Asif maintained that Muslims around the world did not need an agreement to act if the holy sites in Makkah or Madina came under attack. “There is no need to activate any agreement,” he said. The defence minister maintained that Pakistan would fulfil all its obligations under the Makkah Defence Alliance in accordance with the terms of the agreement between the three countries. “There is absolutely no ambiguity,” he asserted. Asked about any military or political engagement with the Houthis, Asif said he could not disclose details, adding that strategies at this level were not meant to be made public. However, he reiterated that Pakistan was bound by the agreement. “Under the trilateral agreement, if the territorial integrity of a country comes under threat, the agreement will be activated and the other two countries will proceed to protect it in fulfilment of their obligations,” he said. “The situation has arrived.” On the US-Israeli war on Iran, Asif said it had become clear, a month into the conflict, that Israel’s calculations had not produced the expected results. “Israel sucked America into this war as a combatant party, but under the present circumstances, the world and the region need to realise that Israel is the real culprit,” he said. “Until Israel is confronted by a joint alliance, it will remain a threat to the region. The Zionist lobby also forces the US to join Israel’s wars.” Sharing his personal view on possible Iranian support for the Houthis, he said Iran, as a state, might not be backing the group as it was already embroiled in another conflict in the Middle East. “This would be a diplomatic error if Iran were to take the side of the Houthis, but the chances are minimal. Escalating the conflict into another theatre is not a wise decision and could turn it into a wider conflict,” Asif said. Fresh fighting between the Houthis and the Yemeni government has dragged in Riyadh, with the Houthis declaring a maritime blockade on the kingdom and targeting its ships in the Red Sea. Last week’s lightning offensive saw the group seize control of the entirety of Yemen’s Red Sea coast and the Bab al-Mandab Strait, a vital artery for Saudi oil exports as the wider Middle East war chokes off the Strait of Hormuz strategic shipping route. Pakistan’s stance Earlier today, Inter-Services Public Relations (ISPR) Director General Lieutenant General Ahmed Sharif Chaudhry said that the defence alliance has no “regional aspirations”, adding that it is intended for collective deterrence. The military spokesperson made the remarks during an interview on Al Arabiya English’s programme ‘Global News Today’, during a conversation with the host, Tom Burges Watson. “It formalises Pakistan’s decades-old relationship with the kingdom of Saudi Arabia and the brotherly country of Turkiye in the domains of collective deterrence and defence,” he said. Watson asked whether the pact was primarily a defensive cooperation or the beginning of a broader strategic alliance. To that, Lt Gen Chaudhry asserted that the pact was defensive, as its name implied. “It is defensive. There’s nothing aggressive. There are no regional aspirations. It is collective deterrence,” he said, adding that the agreement was also “complementary”. During the interview, Lt Gen Chaudhry was also asked whether he saw the defence agreement becoming a part of the wider, Muslim-world security architecture. He replied that there was nothing in the pact that stated that it was a Muslim alliance, adding that it was an alliance for regional stability. “It is not a club that is being made for only Muslim countries,” he said, adding that decisions on its expansion were to be taken by the leadership of Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Turkiye. “This agreement, this alliance can always encompass new, willing partners who also believe in regional peace, stability and security, [and] who have a shared vision of non-aggression, non-interference and collective deterrence. “But that’s for the leadership of these three countries to decide; the how and when part,” he elaborated. The joint defence pact was signed on Aug 7 and provides that an attack on one member state would be treated as an attack on all. Its inaugural meeting was held in Istanbul on Aug 31, where it was decided that Pakistan would initially head the alliance’s secretariat for three years. Since its signing, there has been conversation about the possibility of its expansion, with Turkiye initially suggesting the possibility of Egypt’s inclusion. Though there has been no confirmation from Cairo. From Pakistan, Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif and Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar clarified soon after the signing that the pact was defensive in nature, with the latter saying that it was also “open to any country in the region” willing to uphold its fundamental principles. However, when Foreign Office spokesperson Sajjah Haider Khan was asked about possibility of the pact’s expansion during a weekly media briefing last week, he said an expansion was not on the cards at that point. The three countries first needed to solidify the new organisation before considering opening it to other states with similar threat perceptions and requirements, he explained.

IAEA safeguards deal for Chashma-5 nucle.headline: IAEA safeguards deal for Chashma-5 nuclear power plant secured
IAEA safeguards deal for Chashma-5 nucle.summary: • 1,200MW reactor’s dome placed early; commissioning set for 2028• Talks held with China on N-cooperation ISLAMABAD: The Inte­rnational Atomic Energy Agency and Pakistan on Wednesday signed a safeguards agreement for the 1,200-megawatt Chashma-5 nuclear power plant to bolster the country’s energy security while ensuring international non-proliferation standards. IAEA Director General Rafael Mariano Grossi and Pakistan Atomic Energy Commission Chairman Raja Ali Raza Anwar signed the pact at the agency’s headquarters in Vienna. The signing took place on the sidelines of the 70th IAEA General Conference. Shan Zhongde, chairman of the China Atomic Energy Authority, witnessed the ceremony. The agreement, which governs the application of safeguards at Unit-5 of the Chashma plant, was unanimously approved by the IAEA Board of Governors in March. According to a statement on the signing, the agreement marks a critical step toward implementing safeguards for the new facility. Officials noted that it reflects the international community’s continued confidence in Pakistan’s commitment to the peaceful use of nuclear energy and its adherence to global non-proliferation obligations. Construction of the Chashma-5 (C-5) facility is progressing rapidly, with early completion of the reactor’s dome placement among its recent milestones. Scheduled for commissioning in 2028, the unit is expected to add a substantial source of low-carbon, low-cost electricity to Pakistan’s national grid to support climate objectives and sustainable economic growth. Pakistan currently operates six nuclear power plants with a combined installed capacity of 3,530 megawatts. According to the Atomic Energy Commission, these plants have maintained an average capacity factor exceeding 90pc. Officials highlighted that the country possesses more than 100 reactor-years of operational experience, maintaining a strong record of safe, secure and safeguarded operations under international standards. Prior to the signing ceremony, Pakistani and Chinese delegations met to discuss ongoing and future cooperation in the peaceful applications of nuclear science and technology. Anwar led the Pakistani delegation, while Zhongde headed the Chinese group. Mohammad Kamran Akhtar Malik, Pakistan’s ambassador to Austria and permanent representative to the IAEA, also participated in the bilateral discussions. Published in Dawn, September 17th, 2026

story_clusters.representative_headline: Pakistan committed to implementing Saudi defence pact, Makkah agreement: FO

articles.headline: Pakistan committed to implementing Saudi defence pact, Makkah agreement: FO
articles.summary: Pakistan on Thursday said it remained committed “in intent and spirit” to implementing the Strategic Mutual Defence Agreement (SMDA) with Saudi Arabia and the trilateral Makkah Defence Alliance. Foreign Office (FO) spokesperson Sajjad Haider Khan made the statement during his weekly briefing. The statement comes amid renewed tensions in the Middle East, with Yemen’s Houthi rebels carrying out attacks in Saudi Arabia in recent days. A day earlier, a Saudi-led coalition battling Houthis accused the rebels of targeting the holy city of Makkah, sparking outrage across the Muslim world and deepening the conflict roiling the region. However, the Houthis swiftly rejected Riyadh’s report as a “lie” that it shot down a drone from the rebels heading towards Makkah. In response to a question on whether “any mechanism had been devised as to how Pakistan will ensure that recent Houthi attacks in Saudi Arabia are thwarted,” the spokesperson said that Pakistan was committed to “implementing” the SDMA and the Makkah pact. “However, when, how, where and what force will be used against what objectives, in which modes and matters [..] — operational confidentiality requires us to be discreet at this stage,” he added. Asked about the diplomatic efforts undertaken by Pakistan to “de-escalate and defuse” the Houthi issue, the spokesperson said, “Pakistan has for a long time [..] shared the perspective that we would like to have peace and stability because this is not only in the interest of Pakistan and Iran, but also the entire region and beyond.” Khan termed the situation in Bab al-Mandeb “exceptionally serious” and went on to call on the Houthis to “stop their activities”. “In this regard, our discussions basically revolve around bringing peace and stability through dialogue and diplomacy and not through coercive measures,” he added. PM Shehbaz to head to US next week for UNGA In his press briefing, the spokesperson also confirmed that Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif will be leading Pakistan’s delegation at the 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly (UNGA) in New York next week. Khan said that the premier will be accompanied by Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar and several federal ministers. FO said that in his address at UNGA, PM Shehbaz will “highlight Pakistan’s perspective on regional and global developments, reaffirming the importance of dialogue, diplomacy and restraint and peaceful resolution of issues”. He said the premier is also expected to outline Pakistan’s priorities on sustainable development, climate change, counter-terrorism, Islamophobia, global economic challenges, UN reforms and issues concerning the Global South. He will also draw attention to the situation in India-occupied Kashmir and Palestine, the FO spokesperson said. He added that on the sidelines, PM Shehbaz is scheduled to participate in high-level events and hold bilateral engagements with world leaders and the UN secretary general, where he will highlight “Pakistan’s commitment to multilateralism, the UN Charter, regional peace and international cooperation”. ‘Malicious media campaign’ against Pakistan on Sikh pilgrims The spokesperson was also asked about media reports regarding Pakistani Sikh pilgrims who were stopped at Faisalabad International Airport while travelling to India to perform religious rituals at Gurdwara Sri Hemkund Sahib. In response, he termed it a “malicious media campaign” on India’s part and clarified, “It was reported that the pilgrims were not allowed to board the plane, which is not correct.” “We were not aware that the Indian High Commission had issued these visas, and the visas were not covered under the 1974 bilateral protocol that exists between Pakistan and India,” he said, explaining that protocol’s objective was to facilitate visits to shrines between both countries. Khan said the visas were issued “independently of any coordination”. Noting India’s “exceptionally restrictive visa regime,” the spokesperson said Pakistan was committed to “extending a warm welcome to Sikh pilgrims in Pakistan, including from India”. He also cited the number of visas issued to Sikh pilgrims over various religious occasions, stating that the “numbers speak for themselves”. He noted that Indian Sikh pilgrims had been barred by their country from travelling to Pakistan in 2025. Khan also maintained that Pakistan was ready to welcome Sikh pilgrims through the Kartarpur corridor “as and when India allows them because it has been closed from the Indian side and not Pakistan”. Khan was also asked about India’s participation at the 12th meeting of the Heads of Border Services of the Competent Authorities of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO). In this regard, the spokesperson confirmed that India’s chargé d’affaires was present at the summit. “Participation is there, and we hope that participation will continue because the broader objective is peace and security and fighting terrorism, and it is a common challenge for both countries.” On being asked about India’s response to Pakistan and China operationalising a joint mechanism for managing their common border, the FO spokesperson rejected India’s “baseless and illegally untenable assertions” on the development and the Joint Boundary Demarcation Commission. The Joint Boundary Demarcation Commission was established under the Sino-Pakistan Boundary Agreement of March 2, 1963. According to India’s NDTV, the country’s external affairs ministry had called into question the legality of the commission. “China is not only our neighbour but an all-weather strategic corporate partner. Our ironclad ties have withstood the test of time,” he said. He stressed that the 1963 agreement was “valid”. Khan said that it was a “mockery of international law that India spoke of legality in an attempt to challenge the validity of the border commission”. At this, he said the country should first “carry out its own introspection” over actions in India-occupied Kashmir “instead of advancing fictitious territorial claims”.

story_clusters.representative_headline: India to take 'all necessary measures' to protect economic interests after US passes Russia sanctions bill

articles.headline: India to take 'all necessary measures' to protect economic interests after US passes Russia sanctions bill
articles.summary: India said on Thursday it would continue buying oil from “diversified” suppliers, after US lawmakers approved sanctions designed to squeeze Russia over its war in Ukraine. The US legislation targets Russia’s energy and defence sectors, President Vladimir Putin and other senior officials, as well as Moscow’s so-called shadow fleet of tankers used to circumvent Western sanctions. It also gives US President Donald Trump authority to impose tariffs of up to 100 per cent on major buyers of Russian oil and gas — including potentially China and India — in an effort to choke off revenue financing Moscow’s war. But India’s foreign ministry said it “remains firmly committed to ensuring energy security for its 1.4 billion people”. “It will continue to do so through diversified sourcing and on the basis of evolving market dynamics.” Moscow is one of New Delhi’s most important strategic partners and military suppliers. “The Indian side has also made clear its determination to take all necessary measures to protect its trade and economic interests,” the ministry added. India has navigated the energy crisis caused by the US-Iran conflict in part by turning to Russia, despite Moscow’s war in Ukraine and pressure from Washington and other Western capitals. Putin and Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi held talks in New Delhi last week ahead of a Brics summit. “This issue has been discussed at high levels in recent months with various US interlocutors,” the ministry added. “Its potential implications for not just the bilateral relationship but also the international energy market have been very clearly articulated by the Indian side.” Indian refiners nearly doubled crude imports from Russia to 2.25 million barrels a day in March — the weeks after the Middle East war erupted — helped by temporary US waivers. Shipments hit a record 2.81m in July, according to trade intelligence firm Kpler, but have since dropped back to 2.07m last month.

story_clusters.representative_headline: ‘Belligerent action’: Pakistan protests Indian Navy vessel’s 'provocative' manoeuvre near PN vessel

articles.headline: ‘Belligerent action’: Pakistan protests Indian Navy vessel’s 'provocative' manoeuvre near PN vessel
articles.summary: Pakistan on Wednesday summoned the Charge d’Affaires of the Indian High Commission and lodged a “strong protest” over a “highly provocative and unacceptable” action by an Indian Navy vessel in Pakistan’s Exclusive Economic Zone (EEZ) on Sept 15, the Foreign Office (FO) said. According to the FO, the incident occurred while the Pakistan Navy was conducting its biennial exercise, SEASPARK-26. The FO said that the Indian vessel carried out “aggressive manoeuvres” in dangerously close proximity to a Pakistani naval ship, resulting in contact between the two vessels. The ministry termed the incident a “serious violation of international law” as well as the 1991 bilateral agreement on Advance Notice on Military Exercises, Manoeuvres and Troop Movements. It said the incident also risked escalating tensions in the region. The Indian diplomat was asked to convey to New Delhi that Pakistan “strongly rejects” the “belligerent Indian action” and urged India to strictly adhere to international law and bilateral agreements, particularly those intended to prevent incidents at sea. The FO added that Pakistan’s Charge d’Affaires in New Delhi would lodge a similar demarche with India’s Ministry of External Affairs. Pakistan also called on the international community to urge India to refrain from what it described as “irresponsible actions” that could further destabilise South Asia. “The region can ill-afford to remain perpetually hostage to India’s reckless pursuit of conflict and instability,” the ministry said. India’s Ministry of External Affairs also summoned Pakistan’s envoy in New Delhi earlier today and issued a demarche over the incident. In May 2025, a four-day conflict between Pakistan and India was sparked by an attack on tourists in occupied Kashmir’s Pahalgam, which New Delhi, without evidence, linked to Pakistan. Islamabad strongly denied responsibility while calling for a neutral investigation. After New Delhi launched deadly air strikes in Punjab and Azad Kashmir on May 7, Pakistan said it downed six Indian planes in air-to-air combat, later raising the tally to eight. After tit-for-tat strikes on each other’s airbases, it took American intervention on May 10 for both sides to finally reach a ceasefire. In April, on the first anniversary of the Pahalgam attack, Pakistan had rejected a renewed Indian propaganda campaign linking it to the attack, deploring that the neighbouring country was focusing on “weaponising its false narrative” in the midst of a regional crisis sparked by the US-Israel war on Iran.

story_clusters.representative_headline: US drone maker Powerus says it signed MoU with Pakistan Army, gets initial order

articles.headline: US drone maker Powerus says it signed MoU with Pakistan Army, gets initial order
articles.summary: US drone firm Powerus has signed a memorandum of understanding (MoU) with the Pakistan Army that includes an initial drone-related order, co-founder Brett Velicovich told Reuters on Wednesday. Velicovich declined to provide details, citing security sensitivities, but said the deal fell within the category of unmanned aerial systems. He also declined to disclose the value of the order, citing confidentiality. Powerus, which offers aerial and maritime drones for military and industrial use, is due to merge with a publicly traded company backed by two of US President Donald Trump’s sons, called Aureus Greenway Holdings. Both companies have said they expect the merger to complete in early October. Trump’s sons, Donald Trump Jr and Eric Trump, own a stake in Aureus through an investment fund called American Ventures, according to US regulatory filings. American Ventures is expected to hold a 9.9 per cent beneficial ownership stake in the combined company after the merger, regulatory filings show. Inter-Services Public Relations on Wednesday said a Powerus delegation led by Velicovich met Chief of Defence Forces (CDF) and Chief of Army Staff Field Marshal Asim Munir and they discussed defence procurement, production and long-term capacity building. The statement did not mention the MoU. The military’s media wing did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the agreement outside business hours. Andrew Fox, Powerus’ founder and chief executive, said that Pakistan’s private defence sector remains “emerging but still not mature”, leaving room for US firms to move faster. “The goal would be a joint technology relationship, pairing best-in-breed technology from the US with best-in-breed technology from Pakistan,” Velicovich said, adding that Powerus was exploring ways to potentially build technology in Pakistan. Fox dismissed suggestions that the company’s growth was linked to the involvement of the Trump sons, saying contracts were awarded on merit and that they had “no involvement on the business side” of the company. Donald Trump Jr was a passive investor with an indirect holding, his spokesperson said. “Don has no involvement whatsoever in the management or operations of Powerus and plays absolutely no role in the procurement of contracts in the United States or abroad,” the spokesperson said. “He had no prior knowledge of this deal and had no involvement of any kind in its negotiation, procurement or execution.” Eric Trump could not immediately be reached. White House Special Assistant to the President and Principal Deputy Press Secretary Anna Kelly said, “There are no conflicts of interest.”

story_clusters.representative_headline: Will respond to terror threats from Afghanistan in self-defence as and when needed, Pakistan tells UNSC

articles.headline: Will respond to terror threats from Afghanistan in self-defence as and when needed, Pakistan tells UNSC
articles.summary: WASHINGTON: Pakistan told the UN Security Council on Wednesday that it would respond to terrorist threats emanating from Afghanistan in self-defence as and when needed and in accordance with international law. The assertion by Pakistan’s Permanent Representative to the United Nations Asim Iftikhar Ahmad came during a Security Council meeting on the situation in Afghanistan five years after the Taliban’s takeover of Kabul. “Pakistan cannot sit idle in the face of this terrorist onslaught,” Ahmad told the UNSC. “We will respond in self-defence, as and when needed and in accordance with international law. We will defend ourselves against whosoever attempts to harm our citizens and our national security.” He said that more than 4,700 Pakistanis had lost their lives to terrorism emanating from Afghanistan over the past three years and added that Kabul had failed to take concrete and verifiable action against terrorist groups operating from Afghan soil. Afghanistan had again become a safe haven for terrorist groups including the banned Tehreek-i-Taliban Pakistan, Baloch Liberation Army and its Majeed Brigade, Islamic State-Khorasan and the East Turkestan Islamic Movement, as well as their affiliates, Pakistan’s envoy said. “The situation [is] made worse by external actors, the spoilers who support proxies inside Afghanistan to target Pakistan and other neighbouring countries,” he added. A recent report by UN Secretary General Antonio Guterres says terrorist groups remain present in Afghanistan, while restrictions on women and girls, exclusionary governance, economic pressures, declining capacity to provide basic services and large-scale returns and migration continue to threaten the country’s longer-term stability. Armed groups opposed to the Taliban also remain active. According to the report, such groups claimed responsibility for 88 attacks across 21 Afghan provinces between May 1 and the end of July. The report identifies the institutionalised denial of the rights of women and girls and the authoritarian nature of the Afghan Taliban’s political system among the most serious concerns. It says these policies affect Afghan society and remain obstacles to the country’s reintegration into the international system. Against this backdrop, Ahmad said Islamabad had supported Afghanistan’s stabilisation through engagement, humanitarian assistance and regional cooperation. “Despite reservations with regard to certain policies of the Afghan Taliban, Pakistan abided by its international commitments to allow unhindered humanitarian aid to Afghanistan. As noted in the secretary general’s report, at least 687 humanitarian cargo trucks entered Afghanistan from Pakistan during the reporting period,” he said. But, “unfortunately, the hopes and expectations of the international community at that critical juncture five years ago did not materialise and in fact gradually turned into despair and disappointment”. “The extent of challenges in Afghanistan is evident … and the secretary general’s report highlights that the semblance of relative stability that the Taliban seek to display ‘masks the accumulating risks that could impact the country’s stability over the short and long term’“, he said. Ahmad said terrorism had been at the “core of Afghanistan’s problems”. “This finds its roots in the deep nexus between the Taliban and terrorist groups,” he said, adding that the Afghan Taliban had failed to act against the terrorist groups. He further warned about weapons left behind in Afghanistan by international forces and illegal arms trafficking. The United States took a similarly critical position on the Afghan Taliban, with Ambassador Mike Waltz focusing on the detention of American citizens, terrorism and restrictions on women and girls. “The United States will not tolerate the Taliban taking American citizens hostage. Period,” Waltz said, accusing the Afghan Taliban of using American citizens as bargaining chips. He called on the Security Council to condemn the detention of US citizens by the Afghan Taliban and demand their release. Waltz also criticised the Taliban’s sheltering of terrorist groups and cited UN reporting on arbitrary arrests and detention, torture, ill-treatment and extrajudicial killings. He highlighted the continuing ban on girls’ education beyond sixth grade and restrictions preventing Afghan women working for the United Nations from entering UN compounds. The envoy questioned how long the international community could continue relying on engagement without seeing concrete changes. “How many UN reports documenting abuse? How many Council resolutions demanding change? How many years of ‘engagement’ can we pass before we see measurable results?” he asked. “This Council must demand results from the Taliban,” Waltz said. “We need to see action, not words.” Russia, on the other hand, argued that engagement rather than pressure remained essential in Afghanistan’s case. Ambassador Vassily Nebenzia said there was “no alternative” to genuine, pragmatic engagement with Afghanistan. Recalling the withdrawal of foreign forces five years ago, he said predictions that Afghanistan would collapse or become a “black hole” had not materialised. Nebenzia attributed the country’s relative stability to the Taliban’s focus on development, regional cooperation and building a self-reliant state. He called for trust-based dialogue with the Afghan authorities, “fully free from the language of pressure and blackmail”. China also argued for continued engagement while acknowledging concerns over the treatment of women. Deputy Ambassador Sun Lei urged all parties to “cherish the outcomes of engagement and dialogue with the Afghan government, show good faith and stay patient”. But he said restrictions imposed on Afghan women and girls affected their physical and mental health and undermined social stability and development prospects, making it harder for Afghanistan to gain greater international support. China called on the Afghan rulers to guarantee the fundamental rights and interests of all Afghans, including women. Seemingly referring to the US, it called on a “relevant country” to “bear its historical responsibilities” by resuming aid to Afghanistan, lifting unilateral sanctions, returning the overseas assets of the Central Bank of Afghanistan and providing resources for the country’s reconstruction and development. The debate highlighted the central disagreement over how the international community should deal with Afghanistan five years after the Taliban takeover.

story_clusters.representative_headline: Security forces kill 3 terrorists in Balochistan's Awaran district: state media

articles.headline: Security forces kill 3 terrorists in Balochistan's Awaran district: state media
articles.summary: Security forces killed three terrorists in an intelligence-based operation (IBO) in the Badrang area of Balochistan’s Awaran district, state-run Radio Pakistan reported on Thursday. A large quantity of weapons and ammunition was recovered from the possession of the terrorists of Fitna al Hindustan, according to security sources cited by Radio Pakistan. Fitna al Hindustan is a term designated by the state for terrorist organisations in Balo­chistan. Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi praised security forces for the “successful operation conducted under Operation Radd-ul-Fitna 3”, state-run APP reported. In a statement, the minister said the operation reflected the capability and commitment of the forces in dealing with security threats. He affirmed that security forces remain determined to maintain peace in Balochistan and continue efforts to counter terrorism. He noted that personnel deployed in different areas of the province were carrying out their responsibilities with commitment and resolve. Naqvi noted that security forces had once again foiled terrorists’ plans through timely action. The minister further said that the complete elimination of terrorists and their facilitators was the demand of the entire nation. He said all institutions were working toward this objective, and efforts will continue to address security challenges. Terror attacks in Balochistan Balochistan has witnessed an increase in terrorist attacks in recent weeks, prompting security forces to intensify counter-terrorism operations. Last month, the number of terrorist attacks in the province increased by seven per cent from 83 in July to 89 in August, according to a monthly assessment by the Pakistan Institute for Conflict and Security Studies. On the night of Aug 31-Sept 1, terrorists of the banned Tehreek-i-Taliban Pakistan (TTP) launched a coordinated attack on the Customs House, located at Ziarat Cross on the N-50 National Highway, in the Pishin district. In retaliatory action, security forces killed 10 terrorists while two officers were among six martyred in the fire exchange, according to the military’s media affairs wing. Also on August 31, 11 terrorists belonging to Fitna-al-Hindustan, who had blocked the N-40 Quetta-Taftan highway by establishing an illegal checkpoint for extortion in Chagai’s Nokcha area, were killed following an intense exchange of fire. On September 2, security forces killed 12 terrorists in the Kalat district during an IBO. Days later, the troops killed 11 terrorists and recovered 2.9 tonnes of explosives during separate IBOs in Kharan and Washuk districts. Another 36 terrorists were eliminated during multiple “high-tempo” operations conducted in Mastung, Quetta, Kalat and Sibi districts, the Inter-Services Public Relations said on September 4. These also included thwarting an attack on a police station in Sibi’s Bhag area. On Monday, nine terrorists, including a key commander of a banned outfit, were killed by security forces and the Balochistan Counter-Terrorism Department in two separate operations in Mastung, Pishin and Qila Abdullah districts.

story_clusters.representative_headline: Pakistan to stand by Saudi Arabia 'practically and diplomatically' if Yemen conflict escalates: Asif

articles.headline: Pakistan to stand by Saudi Arabia 'practically and diplomatically' if Yemen conflict escalates: Asif
articles.summary: Defence Minister Khawaja Asif on Wednesday said Pakistan would “practically and diplomatically” stand by Saudi Arabia against Yemen’s Houthi rebels if the situation escalated. Earlier in the day, the Saudi-led coalition battling Yemen’s Houthis accused the rebels of targeting the holy city of Makkah, sparking outrage across the Muslim world and deepening the conflict roiling the region. However, the Houthis swiftly rejected Riyadh’s report as a “lie” that it shot down a drone from the rebels heading towards Makkah. “If the situation escalates, we will stand with Saudi Arabia, both practically and diplomatically,” he said while speaking on Geo News programme ‘Aaj Shehzaib Khanzada Ke Saath’. Commenting on the Pakistan-Turkiye-Saudi Arabia trilateral agreement — the Makkah Defence Alliance — he affirmed that an agreement was in place. However, he said that even if there had been no such agreement, Pakistan was bound by an “eternal agreement to respond if the holy sites come under attack”. “There are some worldly agreements, too, and they have their own sanctity and obligations, but protecting the holy sites is our religious duty,” he said. Asif maintained that Muslims around the world did not need an agreement to act if the holy sites in Makkah or Madina came under attack. “There is no need to activate any agreement,” he said. The defence minister maintained that Pakistan would fulfil all its obligations under the Makkah Defence Alliance in accordance with the terms of the agreement between the three countries. “There is absolutely no ambiguity,” he asserted. Asked about any military or political engagement with the Houthis, Asif said he could not disclose details, adding that strategies at this level were not meant to be made public. However, he reiterated that Pakistan was bound by the agreement. “Under the trilateral agreement, if the territorial integrity of a country comes under threat, the agreement will be activated and the other two countries will proceed to protect it in fulfilment of their obligations,” he said. “The situation has arrived.” On the US-Israeli war on Iran, Asif said it had become clear, a month into the conflict, that Israel’s calculations had not produced the expected results. “Israel sucked America into this war as a combatant party, but under the present circumstances, the world and the region need to realise that Israel is the real culprit,” he said. “Until Israel is confronted by a joint alliance, it will remain a threat to the region. The Zionist lobby also forces the US to join Israel’s wars.” Sharing his personal view on possible Iranian support for the Houthis, he said Iran, as a state, might not be backing the group as it was already embroiled in another conflict in the Middle East. “This would be a diplomatic error if Iran were to take the side of the Houthis, but the chances are minimal. Escalating the conflict into another theatre is not a wise decision and could turn it into a wider conflict,” Asif said. Fresh fighting between the Houthis and the Yemeni government has dragged in Riyadh, with the Houthis declaring a maritime blockade on the kingdom and targeting its ships in the Red Sea. Last week’s lightning offensive saw the group seize control of the entirety of Yemen’s Red Sea coast and the Bab al-Mandab Strait, a vital artery for Saudi oil exports as the wider Middle East war chokes off the Strait of Hormuz strategic shipping route. Pakistan’s stance Earlier today, Inter-Services Public Relations (ISPR) Director General Lieutenant General Ahmed Sharif Chaudhry said that the defence alliance has no “regional aspirations”, adding that it is intended for collective deterrence. The military spokesperson made the remarks during an interview on Al Arabiya English’s programme ‘Global News Today’, during a conversation with the host, Tom Burges Watson. “It formalises Pakistan’s decades-old relationship with the kingdom of Saudi Arabia and the brotherly country of Turkiye in the domains of collective deterrence and defence,” he said. Watson asked whether the pact was primarily a defensive cooperation or the beginning of a broader strategic alliance. To that, Lt Gen Chaudhry asserted that the pact was defensive, as its name implied. “It is defensive. There’s nothing aggressive. There are no regional aspirations. It is collective deterrence,” he said, adding that the agreement was also “complementary”. During the interview, Lt Gen Chaudhry was also asked whether he saw the defence agreement becoming a part of the wider, Muslim-world security architecture. He replied that there was nothing in the pact that stated that it was a Muslim alliance, adding that it was an alliance for regional stability. “It is not a club that is being made for only Muslim countries,” he said, adding that decisions on its expansion were to be taken by the leadership of Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Turkiye. “This agreement, this alliance can always encompass new, willing partners who also believe in regional peace, stability and security, [and] who have a shared vision of non-aggression, non-interference and collective deterrence. “But that’s for the leadership of these three countries to decide; the how and when part,” he elaborated. The joint defence pact was signed on Aug 7 and provides that an attack on one member state would be treated as an attack on all. Its inaugural meeting was held in Istanbul on Aug 31, where it was decided that Pakistan would initially head the alliance’s secretariat for three years. Since its signing, there has been conversation about the possibility of its expansion, with Turkiye initially suggesting the possibility of Egypt’s inclusion. Though there has been no confirmation from Cairo. From Pakistan, Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif and Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar clarified soon after the signing that the pact was defensive in nature, with the latter saying that it was also “open to any country in the region” willing to uphold its fundamental principles. However, when Foreign Office spokesperson Sajjah Haider Khan was asked about possibility of the pact’s expansion during a weekly media briefing last week, he said an expansion was not on the cards at that point. The three countries first needed to solidify the new organisation before considering opening it to other states with similar threat perceptions and requirements, he explained.

story_clusters.representative_headline: IAEA safeguards deal for Chashma-5 nuclear power plant secured

articles.headline: IAEA safeguards deal for Chashma-5 nuclear power plant secured
articles.summary: • 1,200MW reactor’s dome placed early; commissioning set for 2028• Talks held with China on N-cooperation ISLAMABAD: The Inte­rnational Atomic Energy Agency and Pakistan on Wednesday signed a safeguards agreement for the 1,200-megawatt Chashma-5 nuclear power plant to bolster the country’s energy security while ensuring international non-proliferation standards. IAEA Director General Rafael Mariano Grossi and Pakistan Atomic Energy Commission Chairman Raja Ali Raza Anwar signed the pact at the agency’s headquarters in Vienna. The signing took place on the sidelines of the 70th IAEA General Conference. Shan Zhongde, chairman of the China Atomic Energy Authority, witnessed the ceremony. The agreement, which governs the application of safeguards at Unit-5 of the Chashma plant, was unanimously approved by the IAEA Board of Governors in March. According to a statement on the signing, the agreement marks a critical step toward implementing safeguards for the new facility. Officials noted that it reflects the international community’s continued confidence in Pakistan’s commitment to the peaceful use of nuclear energy and its adherence to global non-proliferation obligations. Construction of the Chashma-5 (C-5) facility is progressing rapidly, with early completion of the reactor’s dome placement among its recent milestones. Scheduled for commissioning in 2028, the unit is expected to add a substantial source of low-carbon, low-cost electricity to Pakistan’s national grid to support climate objectives and sustainable economic growth. Pakistan currently operates six nuclear power plants with a combined installed capacity of 3,530 megawatts. According to the Atomic Energy Commission, these plants have maintained an average capacity factor exceeding 90pc. Officials highlighted that the country possesses more than 100 reactor-years of operational experience, maintaining a strong record of safe, secure and safeguarded operations under international standards. Prior to the signing ceremony, Pakistani and Chinese delegations met to discuss ongoing and future cooperation in the peaceful applications of nuclear science and technology. Anwar led the Pakistani delegation, while Zhongde headed the Chinese group. Mohammad Kamran Akhtar Malik, Pakistan’s ambassador to Austria and permanent representative to the IAEA, also participated in the bilateral discussions. Published in Dawn, September 17th, 2026
